topic: How a mould on a forgotten dish led to penicillin
why_chosen: The famous 'lucky mould' story hides a stronger twist: Fleming's mould could never have supplied the world, and the one that did came off a rotten melon from an Illinois market, carried in by someone history still cannot name for certain, which gives one question to carry for ten minutes.
facts_checked: Fleming back at St Mary's on 3 September 1928, mould probably from the mycology lab on the floor below, named penicillin 7 March 1929, paper in British Journal of Experimental Pathology June 1929, two assistants (Ridley and Craddock) tried to extract it and left (Wikipedia, History of penicillin; Science Museum). Lysozyme found 1921 (Fleming biography). Chain left Germany 1933, joined Florey's Oxford department 1935; Oxford team took up penicillin 1939 with Rockefeller funding. Mouse test Saturday 25 May 1940, 8 mice, 4 treated survived, untreated dead by early Sunday; Lancet August 1940 (Wikipedia; Science Museum). Pie dishes, biscuit tins, bedpans, milk churns; about 150 flasks for a small sample; 700 ceramic vessels by James Macintyre and Co, first batch seeded Christmas Day 1940 (Oxford History of Science Museum). Six 'penicillin girls' at two pounds a week (Science Museum). Spores rubbed into coats in case of invasion (Eric Lax, The Mould in Dr Florey's Coat). Albert Alexander, 43, Oxford police constable, first penicillin injection 12 February 1941 at the Radcliffe Infirmary (no dose figure stated because sources disagree), improved within 24 hours, urine recycled, died 15 March 1941 (Wikipedia; Science Museum). Chapter no longer calls him 'the first patient'. Florey and Heatley reached New York 2 July 1941 via Lisbon and met the Peoria (NRRL) team 14 July (HistoryNet). Moyer's corn steep liquor about tenfold yield increase, lactose swap (Wikipedia, Andrew J. Moyer). Worldwide soil and mould search; mouldy cantaloupe from a Peoria market, 1943, strain NRRL 1951, 'parent of all strains used commercially' (USDA-ARS Tellus 'The Enduring Mystery of Moldy Mary'). Mary Hunt's role collecting mould specimens from produce markets is documented; who found the melon is uncertain: Hunt claimed it in a 1962 article, Kenneth Raper credited a Peoria woman who handed it to a guard and left unnamed, and an Abbott advertisement notation names Mary Lou Finley Roberson as 'the original Moldy Mary' (USDA-ARS; Peoria Magazine). X-ray mutant at Cold Spring Harbor 250 to 500 units per millilitre, UV at University of Wisconsin nearly doubled it again (PMC3673487). Pfizer bought an old Brooklyn ice plant for its refrigeration, fourteen deep tanks, opened 1 March 1944 (ACS National Historic Chemical Landmark booklet; EurekAlert). 2.3 million doses for D-Day (UW-Madison; IBMS). Nobel 1945 to Fleming, Florey and Chain; Fleming's Nobel lecture 11 December 1945 quote 'The time may come when penicillin can be bought by anyone in the shops' and warning on underdosing and resistance (NobelPrize.org).
subject: How penicillin went from Fleming's contaminated dish to mass production, and where the mould that actually supplied the world came from
hook_question: If Fleming's famous mould did not make the world's penicillin, where did the one that did come from?
answer: Almost all the world's penicillin descends from a mould found on a rotten cantaloupe from a Peoria, Illinois market in 1943, a strain later boosted by X-rays and ultraviolet and grown in deep tanks, and nobody is certain who carried that melon in.
youtube_title: The Penicillin Mould That Saved Millions Wasn't Fleming's

beats.narration: The mould that saved millions was not Fleming's mould. Nor did it come from a laboratory.
Every schoolchild hears the same story: a busy scientist, a forgotten dish, a lucky blue-green mould, and the age of antibiotics begins.
But in February 1941, the entire penicillin supply in Oxford could not save one policeman.
Three years later, factories in America had two point three million doses ready for a single invasion.

visual.headline: 2.3 million
visual.sub: penicillin doses prepared for D-Day, June 1944

beats.narration: Somewhere between those two moments, the world quietly swapped the mould that made the medicine.
Fleming's famous strain was pushed aside by one from a place you would never guess.
Scientists on two continents spent years chasing a problem that luck alone could not fix.
And the person who found that mould has never been identified for certain.
So if Fleming's mould did not make the world's penicillin, where did the real one come from?
London, the third of September, 1928. Alexander Fleming comes back from his summer holiday to a cluttered bench at Saint Mary's Hospital.
Before leaving, he had stacked dishes of Staphylococcus, the germ behind boils and many wound infections.
One dish had grown a fuzzy blue-green mould, and around it, the germ colonies had turned see-through and were breaking apart.

visual.headline: The contaminated dish
visual.model: glass petri dish with a blue-green mould patch and pale bacterial colonies

beats.narration: He knew what that might mean. In 1921 he had found lysozyme, a germ-killer in tears, but it mostly killed harmless germs.
The spores had probably drifted up from a mould laboratory on the floor below.
Fleming grew the mould in broth and found its juice killed many dangerous germs, yet did not seem to harm animals.
On the seventh of March, 1929, he named it penicillin, and that June he published his results.
His paper even suggested it might be used on infected wounds, yet almost nobody followed it up.
The trouble was that the substance was fragile and hard to purify, and it lost its strength quickly.

visual.headline: Too Fragile
visual.sub: hard to purify, quick to weaken

beats.narration: His two young assistants tried to extract it, then both left for other jobs.
So Fleming kept the mould alive, but used it mostly as a laboratory tool for sorting one germ from another.
The cure sat in Fleming's cultures, and the world walked past it for ten years.
Then a refugee chemist in Oxford came across Fleming's old paper while searching the journals.
Why would anyone dig up an old paper that its own author had set aside?
Ernst Chain had left Germany in 1933, and by 1935 he was working in Howard Florey's pathology department at Oxford.
The two were studying natural substances that kill bacteria, and penicillin looked like a puzzle worth solving.
By 1939, the Oxford team had taken up penicillin, soon backed by a grant from America's Rockefeller Foundation.
A young biochemist, Norman Heatley, built the equipment to coax the fragile drug out of the broth.
Then, on Saturday the twenty-fifth of May, 1940, they infected eight mice with deadly streptococcus bacteria.
Four of the mice received penicillin. The other four were given nothing at all.
Heatley stayed up through the night to watch, and by the early hours of Sunday, the untreated mice were dead.
By morning, all four treated mice were still alive. The drug had worked inside a living body.

visual.headline: Still Alive
visual.sub: all four treated mice, that morning

beats.narration: The results appeared in The Lancet in August 1940. But a mouse weighs about twenty grams, and a man is roughly three thousand times heavier.

visual.headline: 3,000 times
visual.sub: how much heavier a man is than a mouse

beats.narration: Treating people would need vast amounts of mould broth, and British drug companies, stretched by the war, would not take it on.
So Florey made a bold decision: he would turn his university department into a factory.
Oxford's first penicillin factory ran on pie dishes, biscuit tins, milk churns and hospital bedpans.
Around one hundred and fifty flasks of culture were needed for just one small sample of the drug.

visual.headline: 150 flasks
visual.sub: of culture for one small sample

beats.narration: Bedpans turned out to work well, giving the mould a wide, shallow surface of broth to grow on.
So Heatley designed a stackable ceramic vessel, and a Staffordshire pottery firm, James Macintyre, made seven hundred of them.

visual.headline: Heatley's culture vessel
visual.sub: 700 made by James Macintyre and Co.
visual.model: flat rectangular white ceramic culture vessel with a short spout on top

beats.narration: The first batch was seeded with mould spores on Christmas Day, 1940.
To tend them, the team hired six young women, later known as the penicillin girls, for two pounds a week.
They seeded the vessels, waited days for the mould to grow, and drained off broth that held only a trace of the drug.

items.label: Drain
items.text: broth with a trace of drug

beats.narration: Heatley's clever trick then pulled penicillin out of that broth by changing the acidity of the liquid.
Months earlier, in the summer of 1940, Britain had feared a German invasion, and the team needed a plan in case they had to flee.
They rubbed mould spores into the fabric of their coats, so the mould could survive even if the lab did not.
By early 1941, they had just enough of the drug to try it on a patient with a serious infection.
What happened next proved penicillin worked, and showed exactly why it was not enough.
Albert Alexander was an Oxford police constable in his forties, gravely ill with a severe bacterial infection.
On the twelfth of February, 1941, at the Radcliffe Infirmary, he received his first injection of penicillin.
Within twenty-four hours his fever had dropped, his appetite had returned, and the infection had begun to heal.
It was working. But each day of treatment was draining a tiny supply.
So the team collected his urine, because around eighty percent of a dose leaves the body that way and could be recovered.

visual.sub: of a penicillin dose leaves the body in urine

beats.narration: The Oxford team carried every drop back to the laboratory, determined not to waste a single dose.
The drug was extracted and injected again. Even that was not enough.
After several days the supply ran out, the infection returned, and on the fifteenth of March, 1941, Albert Alexander died.
That was the turn in the story: the medicine had not failed. The supply had.
Penicillin was not the problem. Fleming's mould, growing on the surface of shallow vessels, simply could not make enough of it.
Britain, at war and short of everything, could not build the factories it needed.
So in the summer of 1941, Florey and Heatley packed their mould and set off for a country not yet at war.
On the second of July, 1941, Florey and Heatley landed in New York carrying a precious mould.
They had flown by way of Lisbon, one of the few routes out of wartime Europe.
Within two weeks they were in Peoria, Illinois, at a government laboratory set up to find new uses for farm products.
Its fermentation team already knew how to grow microbes at scale, and Illinois had endless corn.
A scientist there, Andrew Moyer, added corn steep liquor, a sticky leftover from making corn starch, to the mould's broth.

visual.headline: Corn Steep Liquor
visual.sub: a leftover from making corn starch

beats.narration: With that one change, the yield of penicillin jumped about ten times.

visual.headline: 10 times
visual.sub: more penicillin with corn steep liquor

beats.narration: Moyer also swapped the sugar in the recipe for lactose, and the numbers climbed again.
But one limit remained: Fleming's mould grew as a mat on the surface of the broth.
To supply an army, the mould had to grow deep inside huge tanks, stirred and fed with air.
That needed a mould that thrived when submerged and poured out far more penicillin than Fleming's ever could.
So a hunt began. Soil samples and moulds arrived from around the world to be tested.
But the winner, when it came, was not from a distant jungle or mountain. It was much closer to home.
Where do you look for a better mould in a Midwestern city? In its produce markets.
A laboratory technician, Mary Hunt, helped collect mouldy fruit and vegetables from local markets and grow the specimens for testing.
In 1943, a cantaloupe from a Peoria market reached the laboratory, a melon much like our kharbooja, covered in a golden mould.

visual.headline: A mouldy cantaloupe
visual.model: cantaloupe melon with patches of green-gold mould

beats.narration: That was the answer. The mould behind almost all the world's penicillin was not Fleming's. It came from that rotten melon.

visual.headline: A Rotten Melon
visual.sub: parent of all commercial penicillin strains

beats.narration: But who carried it in is disputed. Hunt later said she found it; scientist Kenneth Raper credited a local woman who handed it to a guard and left unnamed.
Even the nickname Mouldy Mary is uncertain: a note on an old Abbott advertisement names a different woman as the original.

visual.headline: Mouldy Mary?
visual.sub: the nickname has more than one claimant

beats.narration: Whoever found it, the melon mould thrived deep in tanks. Scientists then hit its spores with X-rays at Cold Spring Harbor and ultraviolet light at Wisconsin, keeping the best mutants.
Yields rose from two hundred and fifty units per millilitre to five hundred, and ultraviolet nearly doubled that again.
In Brooklyn, Pfizer bought an old ice factory for its refrigeration and turned it into a penicillin plant with fourteen deep tanks, opening on the first of March, 1944.
By June 1944, American factories had two point three million doses of penicillin ready for the Normandy landings.
In 1945, Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize. Heatley, Moyer and whoever found the melon were not among the names.
In his Nobel lecture that December, Fleming warned: 'The time may come when penicillin can be bought by anyone in the shops,' and careless underdosing could make microbes resistant.

visual.headline: The time may come when penicillin can be bought by anyone in the shops.

beats.narration: So Fleming's forgotten dish started the story, but it took a rotten melon from an Illinois market, carried in by someone history cannot name for sure, to finish it.

visual.headline: From a dish to a melon
